case.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017), Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
case.excerpt: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention. The attention used is called "Scaled Dot-Product Attention". The input consists of queries and keys of dimension d_k, and values of dimension d_v. The dot products of the query with all keys are computed, each is divided by sqrt(d_k), and a softmax function is applied to obtain the weights on the values. In practice the attention function is computed on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q; the keys and values are packed into matrices K and V. The matrix of outputs is computed as: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V   (Equation 1). The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to this algorithm except for the scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k). Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. The two are similar in theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can use optimized matrix multiplication. For small d_k the two mechanisms perform similarly, but additive attention outperforms dot-product attention without scaling for larger d_k. The authors suspect that for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients; to counteract this, the dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k). Footnote 4: to illustrate why the dot products get large, assume the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1; then their dot product q . k = sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i has mean 0 and variance d_k.
case.focus: Explain scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Equation 1) using small, editable Q, K, and V matrices. Show similarity scores, normalized attention weights, and the output. Let the learner edit values and switch scaling on/off. Guide them through equal scores and a dominant score. Check that each row of weights sums to one and that the output equals the weighted sum of V. Do not train a Transformer.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows matrix multiplication and dot products but has not studied Transformers.

plan.concept: Scaled dot-product attention: scores $QK^T/\sqrt{d_k}$, softmax weights, weighted sum of $V$.
plan.computation: Given $Q$ ($n\times d_k$), $K$ ($m\times d_k$), $V$ ($m\times d_v$): scores $S = QK^T$, optionally scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, weights $A = \mathrm{softmax}$ over each row of $S$, output $O = AV$.
plan.visual: Left: score matrix heatmap with row-wise softmax arrows; right: weight matrix heatmap and output rows as bars, plus a per-row weight-sum readout.
plan.controls: Number of queries $n$, keys $m$, key dimension $d_k$, value dimension $d_v$, scaling toggle, and editable $Q$, $K$, $V$ matrices.
plan.checks: Each weight row sums to 1; output equals explicit weighted sum of $V$; weights non-negative; scaling divides scores by exactly $\sqrt{d_k}$.

spec.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, by hand
spec.hook: Edit tiny $Q$, $K$ and $V$ matrices and watch similarity scores turn into attention weights and then into the output rows.
spec.idea:
Attention answers a simple question: for each query, which of the stored keys look most similar, and how should I mix their values? We measure similarity with a dot product. If query $q$ and key $k$ point the same way, $q\cdot k$ is large; if they are unrelated, it is near zero.

Raw dot products are not yet weights. We pass each row of scores through a softmax, which exponentiates and renormalizes so the row becomes a probability distribution: all entries non-negative and summing to 1. A large score grabs most of the weight, so the output for that query is mostly the value attached to the best-matching key.

The scaling factor $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ is the 'scaled' in the name. With $d_k$ components, a dot product of independent mean-0 variance-1 vectors has variance $d_k$, so scores grow like $\sqrt{d_k}$ in magnitude. Large scores push softmax into saturation, where its gradients are tiny. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps scores in a well-behaved range.

The output is then just a weighted average of the value rows: $O = AV$. Row $i$ of $O$ is a convex combination of the rows of $V$, with the attention weights as the mixing coefficients.
spec.why: This one equation is the core of the Transformer: every attention head, and every layer of the encoder and decoder, is this computation. Understanding the score-to-softmax-to-weighted-sum pipeline makes multi-head attention, masking and cross-attention readable rather than mysterious.

equations.caption: Equation 1: scale the query-key dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, softmax each row, then multiply by $V$.

equations.tex: S = QK^{\top}, \qquad S_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j = \sum_{t=1}^{d_k} q_{it}\,k_{jt}
equations.caption: The score matrix: entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of query $i$ with key $j$.
Softmax applied along each row of the scaled scores, giving the attention weights.
Output row $i$ is the attention-weighted sum of the value rows.
Footnote 4: with independent mean-0 variance-1 components, the dot product has variance $d_k$, which is why we divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$.

spec.visual_caption: Left panel: the score matrix $S = QK^{\top}$ (scaled if the toggle is on), one row per query, one column per key; darker blue means a larger score. Arrows carry each row into the softmax. Right panel: the attention weight matrix $A$ (each row sums to 1, shown as a readout) and, below it, the output rows $O = AV$ drawn as grouped bars, one group per query, one bar per value dimension. Colours distinguish queries.

explorations.title: Equal scores give uniform weights
explorations.change: Leave $Q$ at all zeros, then drag one entry of $Q$ away from zero.
explorations.observe: With $Q$ all zeros every score in the left heatmap is 0, so every weight in the right heatmap is $1/m$ and each row-sum readout shows 1.000. The output bars sit at the plain average of the value rows. Moving one $Q$ entry breaks the tie and shifts weight toward the best-matching key.
explorations.why: Softmax of a constant vector is uniform: $\exp(c)/\sum_j \exp(c) = 1/m$. Equal similarity means equal attention, and the output is the unweighted mean of $V$.

explorations.title: A dominant score concentrates attention
explorations.change: Turn the scaling toggle off, then back on, and compare the weight heatmap.
explorations.observe: With scaling on, query $q_1 = (3,0)$ scores 3 against $k_1$ and 0 against $k_2$, so after dividing by $\sqrt{2}$ the weights are roughly 0.88 / 0.06 / 0.06 and the output row is close to $v_1$. With scaling off the same scores are 3 and 0, giving weights near 0.95 / 0.02 / 0.02: the row is more peaked and the output is even closer to $v_1$.
explorations.why: Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks the score spread before the exponential, so the softmax is less saturated. That is exactly the effect the paper cites for large $d_k$, where unscaled dot products grow in magnitude and softmax gradients become extremely small.

pitfall.title: The weights are not the output
pitfall.text: The attention weight matrix $A$ is only an intermediate. The output is $O = AV$, a weighted average of the value rows, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$ and has nothing to do with the size of the scores. Changing $V$ leaves $A$ untouched but changes $O$ completely; changing $K$ changes $A$ and therefore $O$.

our_additions: All numeric values in the matrices are toy values chosen for clarity, not from the paper.
The 2x3-style layout, the heatmaps, the row-sum readouts and the output bar chart are our visual choices.
The claim that equal scores give uniform weights $1/m$ is a direct consequence of the softmax formula, stated here as intuition.
The comparison of scaled versus unscaled weights in the second exploration is a toy illustration of the saturation argument, not a reproduction of any experiment in the paper.
grounding.disclaimer: This page is a toy illustration of Equation 1 on tiny hand-editable matrices. It does not train a Transformer and does not reproduce any experiment, dataset or reported number from the paper.
